title: Can a window make electricity and still let you see through it?
blurb: Scientists in Japan made colourless solar windows from thin layers of coloured chemicals. One big window can make about 100 watts.

cover.alt: Mount Fuji hidden behind dark silicon solar panels, and Mount Fuji seen through see-through solar windows
cover.credit: Figure 1, Vohra and Sano, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

source.name: Frontiers for Young Minds
source.title: Colorless Windows That Transform Sunlight Into Electricity

original.title: Ternary active layers for neutral color semitransparent organic solar cells with PCEs over 4%
original.authors: Takashi Sano, S. Inaba, Varun Vohra

cards.b: Most solar panels are made of silicon. They are dark, and you cannot see through them, so they cannot be windows. Scientists can make see-through solar windows from coloured chemicals. But the view through them looks orange or red. Can a solar window make electricity and still show the world in its true colours?

Varun Vohra is an associate professor at the University of Electro-Communications in Japan. He studies special plastics and other materials that carry electricity. Takashi Sano was his student there. Together with a colleague, they published this work in 2019.

They made a layer of colourants 1,000 times thinner than paper. Colourants are chemicals that catch light. They put it between two see-through electrodes, sheets that collect the electricity. Their first windows used two red colourants. These let extra red light through, so the view looked red. So they added a third colourant that catches red light.

img.alt: A diagram of a solar window: a thin active layer between two electrodes, catching light and sending electrons one way
img.credit: Figure 2, Vohra and Sano, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: With three colourants, the window let through about the same amount of red, green and blue light. So colours looked true, just a little darker. The window let through about 43 of every 100 parts of light. An ordinary window lets through about 70. It turned about 4 of every 100 parts of sunlight into electricity. One big window makes about 100 watts.

img.alt: A graph showing red, green and blue light passing equally through the new window, and a view through it beside a normal window
img.credit: Figure 3, Vohra and Sano, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: These are lab results from one team. Oxygen in the air breaks down many colourants, so making windows that last for years is still a challenge. Brighter, stronger windows are hard too. A 500-watt window would look too dark to see through well. The team is now testing new colourants for 250-watt windows.

Most electricity comes from burning coal, gas or oil, which warms our planet. Sunlight is a clean source. Cheap, colourless windows could make electricity on buildings everywhere. A home with a TV, two laptops, a tablet and two phones needs about 212 watts. Three of these windows could run them all at once.

Which colours get through? Divya shines a phone torch at a white wall through a red plastic folder. Then she tries a blue folder, then a clear plastic bag. Which lets the most light through? Which changes the colour most? A red sheet lets red light through. The scientists wanted all colours to pass equally.

Every window already lets sunlight in for free. Should all new buildings have solar windows, even if rooms get a little darker? Or should each family choose for themselves? What would you choose for your own room?

words.m: something that turns sunlight into electricity
a chemical that catches light and gives things colour, like the orange in carrots
a sheet that catches or releases electrons, so electricity can flow
a tiny particle; when electrons flow, that is electricity
a unit for how much electric power something makes or uses
